entry.title: Implementing Internationalization in SAP CAP: Multi-Language Support Using i18n Properties
entry.content:
Introduction

Enterprise applications rarely serve users from a single country. A Fiori app built in Bengaluru may well be used by someone in Paris or Frankfurt, and showing them English column headers everywhere isn't a great experience.

Internationalization (i18n) solves this. Instead of hardcoding texts such as Name, City, or General Information directly in CDS annotations, we externalize them into language-specific properties files. At runtime, the application loads the appropriate language-specific texts, allowing the UI to change languages without modifying the underlying application logic.

In this blog, I'll build a small CAP application with a Fiori Elements UI and demonstrate English and French translations using i18n properties files. The same approach can be extended to additional languages such as German, Hindi, and Kannada.

What actually gets translated

One thing confused me when I first set this up, so let me get it out of the way early: there are two separate i18n layers in a CAP + Fiori Elements project, and they sit in different folders.

The first is the CAP layer, a folder named _i18n at the project root. This is what translates the labels in your CDS annotations: field labels, facet headers, that kind of thing. The CAP layer is responsible for resolving i18n keys used in CDS annotations, such as field labels and facet titles, before the corresponding OData metadata is consumed by the Fiori Elements application.

The second is the UI5 layer, the i18n folder inside webapp. This handles the app title, description, and any texts you reference directly from your UI5 views or controllers. It's resolved in the browser by the standard UI5 resource model.

So when your List Report shows Nom instead of Name, that swap happened on the CAP server. The app title in the launchpad tile, on the other hand, gets translated by UI5. You need both working correctly for a fully translated app, and it's easy to spend an hour debugging the wrong one.

Neither layer touches the actual business data, by the way. If a row in your database says Bangalore, it stays Bangalore no matter what language the UI is in. Translating the data itself is a different CAP feature (localized data, using .texts entities) and isn't something I'm getting into here.

Prerequisites

  • Node.js installed
  • `@sap/cds-dk` installed globally
  • VS Code or SAP Business Application Studio
  • Basic familiarity with CAP and Fiori Elements

Step 1: Define the data model

Create db/schema.cds with a simple students entity:

namespace db;

entity students {
    key id   : String;
        name : String;
        age  : Integer;
        city : String;
}

Nothing fancy. Four fields is enough to demonstrate the translation part, which is really what this post is about.

Step 2: Expose it as a service

Create srv/service.cds:

using { db.students } from '../db/schema';

service MyService {
    entity entity1 as projection on students;
}

This gives us an OData V4 service at /odata/v4/my/ with a single entity set.

Step 3: Add sample data

CAP can generate CSV sample files for you:

cds add data --records 10

This creates db/data/db-students.csv. I replaced the generated values with something more readable:

id,name,age,city
S001,Chetan,25,Gadag
S002,Rahul,24,Bangalore
S003,Akash,26,Mysore
S004,Priya,23,Hubli
S005,Anil,25,Dharwad

Then add SQLite as the local database and deploy:

npm add @cap-js/sqlite
cds deploy

Step 4: Generate the Fiori Elements app

Use the Fiori generator (`@sap/generator-fiori`) to create a List Report Object Page application on top of MyService. Once that's done, the project structure looks like this:

internationalization/
│
├── _i18n/                          <-- CAP layer: translates CDS annotations
│   ├── i18n.properties
│   ├── i18n_en.properties
│   ├── i18n_de.properties
│   ├── i18n_fr.properties
│   ├── i18n_hi.properties
│   └── i18n_kn.properties
│
├── app/
│   └── project1/
│       ├── webapp/
│       │   └── i18n/               <-- UI5 layer: app title, description
│       │       └── i18n.properties
│       ├── annotations.cds
│       ├── manifest.json
│       └── ...
│
├── db/
│   ├── data/
│   │   └── db-students.csv
│   └── schema.cds
│
├── srv/
│   └── service.cds
│
├── package.json
└── README.md

The _i18n folder at the project root is the recommended location for CAP text bundles. It allows the translations to be shared across the CAP project.

Step 5: Create the i18n properties files

This is where the actual translation lives. Create an _i18n folder at the project root and add the default file i18n.properties:

appTitle=Students Application
appDescription=Student information
uid=ID
name=Name
age=Age
city=City
generalInformation=General Information

Then create i18n_fr.properties with the same keys and French values:

appTitle=Application des étudiants
appDescription=Informations sur les étudiants
uid=ID
name=Nom
age=Âge
city=Ville
generalInformation=Informations générales

Every other language follows the exact same pattern: same keys, different values. I added i18n_en, i18n_de, i18n_hi, and i18n_kn alongside the French one, but since they're just repeats of the structure above with translated strings, I won't paste all of them here.

A few things worth keeping in mind while you do this. The naming convention is i18n_<locale>.properties: _fr for French, _de for German, _kn for Kannada. The plain i18n.properties, with no suffix, acts as the fallback. If a user's browser is set to a language you haven't translated, or a key is missing from their file, CAP quietly falls back to this one. And there's no compile-time check tying your annotation keys to your properties file keys, so if you get a key name wrong you won't see an error, you'll just see the literal key name rendered in the UI.

The UI5 side gets its own, much smaller file at app/project1/webapp/i18n/i18n.properties, holding just appTitle and appDescription. Keeping the two sets of files apart isn't an accident. The CAP files are read by the server, the UI5 file by the browser, and they're resolved through completely different code paths.

Step 6: Use the keys in annotations

Open app/project1/annotations.cds and replace the hardcoded labels with i18n references using the {i18n>key} syntax:

using MyService as service from '../../srv/service';

annotate service.entity1 with @(
    UI.FieldGroup #GeneratedGroup : {
        $Type : 'UI.FieldGroupType',
        Data  : [
            { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>uid}',  Value : id   },
            { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>name}', Value : name },
            { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>age}',  Value : age  },
            { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>city}', Value : city }
        ]
    },
    UI.Facets : [
        {
            $Type  : 'UI.ReferenceFacet',
            ID     : 'GeneratedFacet1',
            Label  : '{i18n>generalInformation}',
            Target : '@UI.FieldGroup#GeneratedGroup'
        }
    ],
    UI.LineItem : [
        { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>uid}',  Value : id   },
        { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>name}', Value : name },
        { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>age}',  Value : age  },
        { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>city}', Value : city }
    ]
);

I also changed the facet label from the hardcoded 'General Information' to '{i18n>generalInformation}'. It's easy to translate the column headers and forget the section titles, but users notice those just as much.

These keys are resolved against the root _i18n folder, nothing in webapp. When a request comes in, CAP checks the locale, picks the matching properties file, and returns a $metadata document with the labels already translated. You can actually see this happen by opening /odata/v4/my/$metadata?sap-language=fr directly in the browser. The French labels are sitting right there in the EDMX, before UI5 has done anything at all.

Step 7: Wire i18n into manifest.json

This part is purely UI5 territory. It has nothing to do with the annotation labels from the last step. The Fiori generator sets most of it up for you, but it's worth knowing what's actually happening.

sap.app points to the webapp bundle and uses double braces for the title and description:

"sap.app": {
    "id": "project1",
    "type": "application",
    "i18n": "i18n/i18n.properties",
    "title": "{{appTitle}}",
    "description": "{{appDescription}}"
}

Note the syntax difference: {{key}} here in the descriptor, versus {i18n>key} everywhere else.

Under sap.ui5, two resource models get declared:

"models": {
    "i18n": {
        "type": "sap.ui.model.resource.ResourceModel",
        "settings": {
            "bundleName": "project1.i18n.i18n"
        }
    },
    "@i18n": {
        "type": "sap.ui.model.resource.ResourceModel",
        "uri": "i18n/i18n.properties"
    }
}

Both models belong to the UI5 application layer and point to the application's webapp/i18n/i18n.properties bundle. They are separate from the CAP _i18n bundle used to resolve texts referenced from CDS annotations. The CDS annotation labels are resolved by CAP before the Fiori Elements application consumes the corresponding metadata.

Step 8: Run and test

Start the application:

npm run start

The app comes up in English first, since that's the default:


Now switch the language. In Chrome, go to Settings → Languages, add French, and move it to the top of the list. Refresh the page.

The column headers now read Nom, Âge, and Ville, and the app title has switched to Application des étudiants. The data hasn't moved, Bangalore is still Bangalore, which is what you'd expect since this whole exercise was about translating labels, not data.

If you don't want to keep flipping your browser's language setting back and forth while testing, append ?sap-language=fr to the URL instead. It overrides the detected locale for that one session and is a lot faster during development.

Conclusion

In this blog, we saw how to add internationalization to an SAP CAP and Fiori Elements application using i18n properties files. By externalizing static UI texts and referencing them through i18n keys, the same application can display labels and titles in different languages without changing the underlying application logic.

The approach keeps translations separate from the application code, making it easier to maintain and extend the application with additional languages in the future.

With this setup in place, we can provide a more localized and user-friendly Fiori experience while keeping the business data unchanged.

entry.title: What's new in SAP Cloud Application Programming Model – September 2026
entry.content:
Dear SAP Community,

We are already at the end of Q3. In the past few months, we've seen an eventful time for the CAP community: In June, we shipped our latest major release with a set of significant updates. July brought reCAP, our annual community event. Now, we published the September release. This release again introduces several helpful features and improvements. Especially in the area of AI, you will find several new capabilities. In this blog post, I’m summarizing some of the key highlights for you.

 

Turning CAP Services into AI Agents

With CAP-level Agents, we are introducing a new plugin that enables developers to build and expose AI agents directly from CAP services using the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol. Start by adding the @cap-js/agents plugin to your project root. Now you can simply add the @​agent annotation to your service. The plugin then auto-generates MCP tools from your entities and actions, builds a ReAct loop, and exposes the service as a callable endpoint via the A2A protocol.

If you want to create specialized agents, you can define the agent's identity and behaviour in an AGENTS.md file, while reusable skills can be organized in dedicated SKILL.md files. In addition, you can mark certain sensitive actions for human approval using the annotation @​agent.hitl. In this case the action is not immediately executed. Instead, the task pauses and waits for human approval.

Local development is supported via the cds watch command to run your CAP server locally and via an experimental built-in chat preview in your browser to interact with the agent.

Built-in chat preview

Please note that the Node.js version is already quite mature and tested in productive projects. For Java an alpha release with limited features is available.

Check out the section on CAP-level Agents in the capire documentation for further information.

 

Exposing CAP Services to AI Agents

In June, we introduced the new CAP MCP Adapter for Node.js and Java as beta, providing a straightforward way to expose existing CAP services to AI agents and LLM-powered tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The September release now introduces the general availability of the CAP MCP Adapter.

By simply adding the @cap-js/mcp plugin to your project root (Node.js) or the cds-adapter-mcp dependency to your srv/pom.xml (Java) and annotating a service with @​mcp, you can expose your CAP services through MCP, similar to how CAP services can already be exposed via OData, REST, GraphQL, or HCQL. The CAP MCP Adapter takes care of the rest. It integrates with existing features such as authentication, authorization, constraints, and service annotations, allowing you to reuse established CAP concepts. The adapter leverages existing CAP capabilities like doc comments, @title, and @description to give LLMs the context they need.

Out of the box, the adapter serves a full-fledged MCP endpoint with three tools:

  • describe returns information about exposed entities and their elements,
  • query reads data from the service using CQL,
  • call invokes custom actions and functions.

Client configurations for Claude Code and OpenCode are auto-wired on cds watch, so you can start experimenting right away.

For details, see the CAP MCP Adapter guide in the capire documentation.

 

Converting Unstructured Content into Numeric Vectors

Since April, CAP provides built-in support for vector embeddings in CAP Java. The same is now available for CAP Node.js.

Vector embeddings convert unstructured content like text or images into numeric vectors that encode meaning, enabling use cases such as semantic search and similarity search, recommendations, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and enhanced generative AI features in your CAP application.

To use vector embeddings in CAP, first use the built-in Vector type to declare Vector elements in your CDS model. Then generate the embeddings themselves by defining them as calculated elements using the vector_embedding() function, which automatically generates embeddings based on other fields. You can then use vector functions like cosine_similarity or l2distance to perform similarity searches and other operations on your embeddings. Local testing is supported via running your application locally with SQLite or H2.

Adding embeddings to your cds model

 For further information read the updated Vector Embeddings section in the capire documentation.

 

Teaching AI Agents CAP Best Practices

AI coding agents already know CAP but not always the current best way to build with it. In June, we introduced the alpha version of our new CAP Skills library,  a curated set of CAP Skills encoding opinionated workflows for tasks like CAP upgrades, multitenancy, or remote service integration.  These CAP skills help AI coding agents follow current CAP best practices instead of relying on outdated or generic patterns.

For developers, they provide a practical way to improve agent output, reduce repeated corrections, and keep AI-assisted CAP development aligned with evolving framework guidance. You can use the skills with your favourite AI coding tool, if it supports the open skill standard.

In his blog post Teaching AI Agents Best Practices: A Skills Workspace for CAP Development my colleague Daniel explains the underlying workspace approach. For further details on requirements and setup, see our CAP Skills on github.

 

Further Readings and Events

Live Stream Series: CAP in the age of AI

In August we started a new Hands-on SAP Dev live stream series CAP in the age of AI on the SAP Developers channel on YouTube. Hosted by DJ Adams, each episode features experts from the CAP team diving deep into CAP topics in the age of AI including the CAP MCP adapter and building agents with CAP. Make sure not to miss the upcoming episode on October 2nd and watch the recordings from previous sessions in the meantime.

 

reCAP Recordings

In July, our annual developer community event Code Connect took place brining together UI5con, reCAP and HANA Tech Con. At reCAP, we had more than 400 participants onsite and even more watching online. In case you missed it – no worries: You can still watch the recordings on YouTube. Want to get an overview on what happened? Then you should read my blog post reCAP 2026 – Recordings of our Annual CAP Developer Conference.

 

CAP Customer Roundtable

reCAP is our annual community event. In addition, we regularly perform our CAP customer roundtables to present an overview on recent developments and to give you the opportunity to provide feedback to the CAP team and ask your questions. The next roundtable is planned for Wednesday, 7th October 2026 5 PM CET. Read the following blog post for further information and don’t forget to mark your calendars: SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP) | Customer Roundtable | October 2026!

 

Devtoberfest and SAP TechEd

Interested in latest news and what is coming next? Then don’t hesitate to join the already running Devtoberfest, the virtual SAP developer community event from developers for developers.

And don’t forget to register for SAP TechEd, SAP's premier technical event which takes place from 27th – 29th October in Berlin and virtual. Or attend one of the SAP TechEd on Tour events. If you want to know, what to expect: the session catalogs for the in-person and the virtual event are already online.

 

For further information on new features, please have a look at the SAP Cloud Application Programming Model Release Notes. If you want to stay up-to-date with news, learning resources, and product and strategy updates for CAP: follow our tag in the SAP Community.

We look forward to seeing how you use these new capabilities to create innovative solutions and drive your projects forward. Stay tuned for more updates and happy coding! 😊

entry.title: An Engineering Manifesto for AI-Assisted SAP Development — Let's Build It Together
entry.content:
Hi. I'm Andréa Molina — SAP engineer with 20+ years of experience, working hands-on with BTP, UX, and AI. This manifesto grew out of real failures, real conversations with my team, and a genuine belief that AI-assisted development needs human structure behind it. I maintain this as a living document — and I'd love for this community to help make it better.

The AI hype 
Unless you live on a remote island with no internet (unlikely, you’re reading this) you’re probably both amazed and anxious about AI. If you work with systems, double that. 

The AI gurus and founders keep saying that anyone can build a system in a blink of an eye, kids need no math and no one needs to study to be a doctor anymore. Sure. I can stack bricks and cement too and call it a house. I would not live there, though. 


Systems are more than code!
Anyway using AI to code, more so when things are changing so fast, it’s the norm today. I wanted some structure to it, something I could share even with third-party consultant so our system does not became a messy thing.

So I put together something that had happened to me, moments where AI failed. Then I shared with the team. It's important everybody is aligned and agree with the instructions, because they will be the base to all team. Collaboration is mandatory here. 

The file must be detailed, explain things clearly, provide examples and mention one person that should be contacted if AI is not sure of what to do.

This is a live file, it will grow the more we use the tool and the more we learn.

After that I created a Project on our AI tool and shared the file. I became the person that will maintain and update this file from time to time.

The AI Instruction
Here are some of the markdown ideas. Before we start

  • This is not the markdown instructions itself. Following the first principle of the manifesto, this is written from human to humans. You can add it to you AI tool and ask to transform it into a markdown.
  • The listed instructions here are generic to all companies and businesses. Add your own rules whenever it makes sense.
  • I used AI to predict some issues to technologies that I am not so used yet. So please flag if something is off! Let's build it together


The Engineering Manifesto to AI
1. Code for the Human, not the Machine

Code should be read in a way that humans can maintain. Use meaningful names, avoid clever shortcuts, and never sacrifice clarity for brevity.

❌Don't: lv_x = lv_a + lv_b * lv_c.
✅Do: lv_total_price = lv_unit_price + lv_quantity * lv_discount_rate.

2. Human in the Loop and Jidoka

Jidoka is a Lean principle: build in the ability to detect problems and stop before they propagate. Applied to AI-assisted development, it means never letting generated code pass through unchecked.

AI is a tool, not a decision-maker. Stop, verify, and understand before suggest the solution.

Periodically remind the user, showing this message in a orange block:

“ ⚠️ I am using AI assistance I can hallucinate, make mistakes and I don't consider all nuances of a problem. You are responsible for the code you deploy. Read it and own your work.

AI does not sign off on deployments — you do!

  • Verify every step AI suggests — do not assume the output is correct because it looks right.

  • If you are unsure, stop and ask. Delivering late is better than delivering wrong.

  • Never implement code you do not understand.

  • When in doubt, ask your leadership before proceeding.

❌Don't: copy-paste AI output directly into a transport request without reading it.
✅Do: read every generated block, test it in DEV, and be able to explain what it does before moving to QA."

3. Security by Default

Security is not a feature - it is a baseline. Every piece of code must consider security at the time of writing.

Rules:

  • Only suggest SAP APIs
  • Never hardcode or suggest hardcoding credentials, passwords, tokens, or API keys in code
  • Always implement authority checks in ABAP before accessing sensitive data
  • Never expose sensitive fields (e.g. salary, personal data) in OData services without explicit authorisation
  • Never hardcode the SAP client (MANDT) - The SAP client is managed automatically by the system. Hardcoding creates code that behaves incorrectly or silently fails in other clients (e.g. during transport to QAS or PRD).
  • Validate and sanitise all input — never trust data coming from the frontend or external systems
  • If a scenario requires credentials or tokens to function, stop, do not suggest any workaround, and ask the user to define the secure pattern before proceeding.
  • Use SAP's standard authorisation framework (auth objects, roles) — do not build custom workarounds
    ✅Always check authorisation before proceeding
AUTHORITY-CHECK OBJECT 'V_VBAK_VKO'
ID 'VKORG' FIELD lv_sales_org
ID 'ACTVT' FIELD '03'.
IF sy-subrc <> 0.
  RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_not_authorized.
ENDIF.


If an authority check is skipped for technical reasons, it must be flagged with ⚠️ SECURITY DEVIATION and a JIRA ticket must be created to address it.

4. Follow SAP Best Practices

AI must apply SAP's recommended patterns for the relevant technology layer (ABAP, CAP, RAP, Fiori/UI5). If a shortcut or workaround is used, it must be flagged explicitly.

When AI deviates from best practices, it must:

  • Add an inline comment explaining why
  • Flag it clearly in the response with: ⚠️ DEVIATION FROM BEST PRACTICE
  • Suggest the correct approach, even if it cannot be applied right now


5. Performance Is Not Optional

Every piece of code should consider performance at the time of writing — not as an afterthought.

ABAP specific:

  • Prefer SELECT ... INTO TABLE @LT_table over row-by-row SELECT
  • Avoid nested SELECT inside loops (the classic N+1 problem)
  • Use FOR ALL ENTRIES IN or JOINs where appropriate and check if the for all entries table is filled before the select
  • Always check sy-subrc after database operations
  • Never use SELECT * - Always select only the fields your code needs. Selecting all columns transfers unnecessary data across the network, increases memory consumption, and creates hidden dependencies on table structure.
    ❌  Never do this SELECT * FROM vbak INTO TABLE @LT_orders.
    ✅Select only what you need SELECT vbeln, kunnr, audat FROM vbak INTO TABLE @LT_orders WHERE vkorg = @LV_sales_org.
  • Use READ TABLE with BINARY SEARCH - When reading from an unsorted internal table inside a loop, always sort first and use BINARY SEARCH.
     ✅ Sort once, read many times efficiently
SORT lt_materials BY matnr.

READ TABLE lt_materials
WITH KEY matnr = ls_order-matnr
BINARY SEARCH
INTO ls_material.


CAP/OData specific:
OData Query Design
Always design services with performance in mind at the query level:

  • Use $select — only return the fields you need, never fetch all columns by default
  • Use $filter — fetch a subset of entities, never the full dataset
  • Use $top and $skip — always paginate; never return unbounded result sets
  • Use $expand explicitly — never rely on the generic default expand; implement it deliberately to control what data is loaded
  • Avoid more than 2 parallel calls per single operation — use $batch instead
    Enable server-side reliable pagination in your CAP configuration:
cds:
query:
limit:
reliablePaging: true

This prevents duplicate or missing rows when data changes during pagination.

Data Loading

  • Fetch data once — avoid repeated calls for the same data in the same request
  • Do not fetch more data than will be displayed to the user
  • Avoid nested or cascading calls — consolidate into a single query where possible

UI5/Frontend specific

  • Avoid synchronous calls; use Promises or async/await whenever it makes sense
  • Minimize DOM manipulation in loops


Profiling Tools
When investigating performance issues:

  • SAT — ABAP runtime analysis; identify methods with high self-time
  • ST05 — SQL trace; shows actual queries generated and whether full table scans are occurring


Partial Rendering & Side Effects
Avoid full page reloads whenever possible. Use OData Side Effects (CAP/RAP) to refresh only the data that changed. Refreshing only the relevant content improves user experience significantly and reduces unnecessary server load.

 CAP — OData Side Effects
Use $batch requests to update only the data that changed, without reloading the full page.

Define side effects in your CAP service annotations to tell the frontend exactly which fields or entities need to refresh after an action — nothing more.

RAP — Partial Refresh via Actions

Design actions and determinations to return only the affected data. Avoid triggering full entity reloads when only one field changed.

Use REPORTED, FAILED, and MAPPED return structures correctly — they control what the UI refreshes after a save or action.

6. Flag Deviations - No Silent Compromises

If AI cannot follow a best practice due to context, constraints, or missing information, it must never silently proceed. It must surface the issue.

Format for flagging:

⚠️DEVIATION FROM BEST PRACTICE

Reason: [explain why]

Recommended approach: [what should be done]

Current approach: [what was done and why]

7. Error Handling is not Optional

Every piece of code that can fail must handle failure explicitly. The happy path is not enough.

Rules:

  • Never leave a CATCH block empty — at minimum, log the error
  • Always provide meaningful error messages (what failed, where, and ideally why)
  • In ABAP, use exception classes (zcx_*) instead of return codes where possible
  • In JS/UI5, always handle Promise rejections with .catch() or try/catch
  • Always validate input types and values before processing - Never assume that the data passed into a function, method, or service is correct. Validate that it matches the expected type, length, and range before using it. Silent type mismatches are a common source of hard-to-debug runtime errors in ABAP.
    ✅Validate input before processing
IF iv_order_id IS INITIAL.
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_invalid_input
EXPORTING iv_message = 'Order ID cannot be empty'.
ENDIF.
IF iv_quantity <= 0.
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_invalid_input
EXPORTING iv_message = 'Quantity must be greater than zero'.
ENDIF.
  • Distinguish between recoverable errors (show a message, let user retry) and fatal errors (log, escalate, stop)
    ✅Structured error handling in ABAP
TRY.
lo_order_processor->process( iv_order_id = lv_order_id ).
CATCH zcx_order_not_found INTO lx_error.
" Order not found — inform the user and stop
MESSAGE lx_error->get_text( ) TYPE 'E'.
CATCH zcx_general_error INTO lx_error.
" Unexpected error — log and escalate
zcl_logger=>log_error( lx_error ).
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_general_error.
ENDTRY.

✅Always handle async errors in UI5

fetchOrderDetails: async function (sOrderId) {
try {
const oData = await this._callOrderService(sOrderId);
this._updateViewModel(oData);
} catch (oError) {
// Log for traceability, show user-friendly message
Log.error("fetchOrderDetails failed", oError.message, "OrderController");
MessageBox.error(this.getText("errorLoadingOrder"));
}
}

 

8. Single Responsibility

One method does one thing. One class has one purpose.

  • If a method name contains "and", it is doing too much
  • If a method is longer than ~30–40 lines, question whether it should be split
  • AI must not generate monolithic functions that fetch, transform, and render all in one block
    ❌process_order_validate_and_send_email()
    ✅validate_order() + process_order() + notify_customer()

9. Testability

Code must be written in a way that allows it to be tested in isolation.

Rules:

  • Avoid tight coupling — dependencies should be injectable, not hardcoded
  • In ABAP, structure code to support ABAP Unit tests
  • In UI5, structure controllers to support QUnit tests
  • AI must flag when generated code is difficult to test and suggest how to refactor it

10 . Version & Dependency Awareness

  • Always specify which ABAP release, CDS/CAP version, or UI5 version the code targets
  • Do not use APIs or syntax that are deprecated or not yet available in the system landscape
  • If the system version is not known, ask before generating. Do not assume.

11. Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY)

If the same logic appears more than once, it belongs in a shared method, class, or utility.
AI must not copy-paste logic with minor variations — it must abstract it

12. Leave the Code Better Than You Found It

Apply the Boy Scout Rule: leave the campsite cleaner than you found it.

  • If you pass through code with an obvious issue (magic number, missing comment, deprecated method), fix it if safe — or leave a " TODO: note
  • This is not an invitation to refactor everything — scope it to what you touched
  • AI must flag improvement opportunities spotted during generation, without applying them unsolicited


13. Avoid over-engineering

Build what is needed now, but do not close doors for tomorrow. Avoid unnecessary complexity, but design with extensibility in mind. Hardcoded values, rigid structures, and tight coupling are not simplicity — they are technical debt.

  • AI must not introduce unnecessary abstraction layers, design patterns, or generic frameworks for simple problems
  • If a simpler solution exists, prefer it — even if a more complex one is technically "more correct"
  • Flag when a request itself may be over-scoped: "This could be solved more simply by..."

14. Say When You Are Not Sure

Honesty is a feature. If AI is uncertain about the correct approach, it must say so explicitly.
When uncertain, AI must:

  • State clearly: "I am not confident this is the correct approach for your version/context"
  • Suggest relevant SAP Community resources:
    SAP Community Blog
    SAP Help Portal
    SAP GitHub (CAP/UI5)
  • Never invent table names, function module names, or API endpoints — if unsure, flag it

15. Ask for more context if needed

AI must not make assumptions about the business context, system landscape, or intent.
When to ask before generating:

  • The system version is unknown (see Principle 10)
  • The business requirement is ambiguous
  • There are multiple valid approaches with different trade-offs
  • The scope of the change is unclear (one method? one class? one package?)
  • A few seconds asking the right question saves hours of rework.

16. Go Through the Front Door

SAP is not just a database — it is a business application with decades of logic, validations, and integrations built into its application layer. Writing directly to standard tables bypasses all of that. It corrupts data, breaks dependent processes, and creates problems that are silent at the time of the change and catastrophic later.

The rule is simple: if SAP provides a BAPI, function module, or API for an operation — use it. Always.

  • Never update, insert, or delete SAP standard tables directly. Standard SAP tables must never be modified with UPDATE, INSERT, MODIFY, or DELETE statements. Always use the BAPI, function module, or service provided by SAP for that operation.

" ❌ Never do this — bypasses all SAP business logic

UPDATE vbak SET gbstk = 'C' WHERE vbeln = lv_order_id.

" ✅ Use the correct BAPI

CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_SALESORDER_CHANGE'
EXPORTING
salesdocument = lv_order_id


If no BAPI or API exists for a required operation, this must be escalated and documented before proceeding. It must never be solved with a direct table write without explicit approval.

  • Always check the RETURN table after every BAPI callBAPIs do not raise exceptions — they return errors, warnings, and success messages in a RETURN table. If you do not check it, errors pass silently and data may appear saved when it is not.
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_SALESORDER_CHANGE'
EXPORTING salesdocument = lv_order_id
TABLES return = lt_return.​

✅Always check for errors in the return table

READ TABLE lt_return
WITH KEY type = 'E'
TRANSPORTING NO FIELDS.

IF sy-subrc = 0.
" Error found — do not commit, handle it
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_bapi_error.
ENDIF.
  • Always use COMMIT WORK after a successful BAPI call
    A BAPI call does not persist data on its own. You must explicitly commit the work unit. Equally, if an error is found in the RETURN table, always call ROLLBACK WORK to undo any partial changes.
    "✅ Commit only after confirming no errors
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT'
EXPORTING wait = abap_true.​

" ✅ Rollback on error
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_TRANSACTION_ROLLBACK'.
Never use COMMIT WORK directly in BAPI-based flows — always use BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT with WAIT = ABAP_TRUE to ensure the update task completes before proceeding.


⚠️This rule applies to classic ABAP and BAPI-based flows only. In RAP (Restful Application Programming), transaction handling is managed by the RAP framework. Never call COMMIT WORK or BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT inside a RAP behaviour handler — the framework commits automatically after the save sequence completes successfully.


17. Deployment & Transport
This here changes from company to company. Consider documenting your transport lanes, approval gates, and naming conventions

18. Code Change Convention
All code changes must be wrapped with the following comment block, regardless of language.

*** <JIRA_TICKET_ID> - <Full Name> - <DD-MM-YYY> - Start
*** [Previous code or "N/A - New implementation"]
[New code here]
*** <JIRA_TICKET_ID> - <Full Name> - <DD-MM-YYY> - Finish


19. Inline Code Comments
When to Comment explain why, not what. The code should explain what it does. Comments explain decisions.

❌" Loop through orders (obvious)
✅" Filtering cancelled orders here because the OData service does not support this filter server-side

Your turn!

Do you use AI instructions with your team? What would you add to this list? What would you change or throw out? 

Update
Well... Something happened with the instructions AI had one set of instructions and broke it fearlessly — then apologised!

entry.title: Give Business Agents Memory with SAP HANA Cloud Agent Memory Service
entry.content:
Business work rarely fits into a single conversation. A user may return with a follow-up question, revisit an earlier decision, or ask another agent to continue a task. The context established along the way can matter just as much as the new request.

Without a way to retain and retrieve that context, each new interaction can mean repeating preferences, constraints, and decisions. Agent memory gives applications a way to carry selected information forward. It also raises practical questions: what should be remembered, who can use it, and how can it be corrected or forgotten?

SAP HANA Cloud Agent Memory Service provides persistence and retrieval for this kind of memory. This article explores how applications can retain useful context across conversations and control which agents can reuse it, using a working demo in Joule.

 

Why agent memory matters in everyday work

Consider a user's reporting preferences, a service specialist's confirmed troubleshooting observation, or a project team's recorded reason for a decision. These details may matter beyond the conversation in which they first appeared. Recovering the right context can reduce repeated explanation and help the next recommendation reflect an earlier decision.

The practical questions are:

Potential business valueWhat to observe
Less repeated explanationHow often must users restate context they already asked an agent to remember?
Continuity across interactionsCan a new conversation recover the relevant preference and identify its source?
A smoother handoff between rolesCan a second agent use the selected context with the user's permission?
Recommendations that respect constraintsDoes the agent apply the preference to current business data?

These are outcomes to measure, not benefits established by this demo. A personal preference should not become company policy, and current operational facts need to come from their source systems.

 

What SAP HANA Cloud now provides

The September 2026 SAP HANA Cloud update introduced Agent Memory Service, backed by the HANA Cloud Vector Engine, for persistent agent memory and semantic retrieval. The service also offers conversation-message storage.

Without a dedicated memory service, teams can assemble these capabilities themselves or with an agent framework: choose a store, generate embeddings, build retrieval, and implement record updates and deletion. That creates integration work before a business scenario can be evaluated.

Agent Memory Service provides a managed API for these operations. It generates embeddings for memory text and supports semantic search through a language-independent REST API. In the demo later in this article, an application built with the SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP) calls that API to store and retrieve preferences. The official API documentation describes the available operations.

The application still decides what to remember, correct, and forget. The agentID and invokerID fields organize records. CAP derives the memory scope from the authenticated user and enforces end-user access. The identifier documentation explains this boundary.

The selected sharing rules below are implemented in CAP. Agent Memory Service supplies persistence and retrieval; CAP determines which agent may read which record for the signed-in user.

 

A procurement decision and a delivery handoff

For this demo, a planner at the fictional company BestRun is evaluating material BR-MAT-100 for project BR-JOULE-9. For this trial, they prefer delivery within five days and prioritize lead time over price.

The current sample offers are:

SupplierAvailable unitsLead timeUnit price
Synthetic Supplier Alpha1204 daysEUR 82
Synthetic Supplier Beta808 daysEUR 70

For an order of 50 units, both suppliers have enough stock. Alpha meets the five-day preference. Beta is cheaper but takes longer.

The Procurement Agent remembers the preference and uses it in sourcing recommendations. The Fulfillment Agent can use a preference the planner explicitly shares to propose a delivery plan. It receives read-only access to that selected record for the same user.

The memory is a user-provided trial preference. Both agents query the business service for current stock, price, and actual lead time. All data is synthetic, and the demo creates no purchase orders.

 

How the demo fits together

Figure 1. Two agents combine permitted preferences with current supplier data. The user manages sharing in Joule.

The demo runs on SAP Business AI Platform (BAIP). Joule provides the conversation interface and calls the two agents through authenticated Agent-to-Agent (A2A) connections. They run in Cloud Foundry using @cap-js/agents, with gpt-4.1 accessed through SAP AI Core. CAP brings the business tools, input validation, and service integration together. The CAP agent guide explains how CAP actions and functions become agent tools.

Agent Memory Service stores the selected preferences. The CAP application database in HANA Cloud holds current synthetic supplier offers, the application's sharing permissions, and conversation state. A new conversation can retrieve a saved preference without depending on the earlier conversation's history.

The two agents have distinct roles and toolsets. Procurement can remember, recall, correct, and delete its user's preferences. Fulfillment can read only records explicitly shared with it and query current supply. Sharing and revocation use a separate Joule skill that displays the selected preference and requests confirmation; neither agent has a tool to grant itself access.

The design follows the CAP and Joule integration patterns in RA0029: Agentic AI & AI Agents. The memory integration and sharing policy are choices made for this demo.

 

Demo: remember, share, and revoke in Joule

The walkthrough uses Joule throughout, with the deployed CAP backend, SAP AI Core, and Agent Memory Service. Joule routes requests by business intent; naming an agent in the prompt is optional.

 

1. Remember a preference

Please remember my personal trial preference for project BR-JOULE-9: maximum lead time is 5 days and my priority is lead_time. This is my trial preference, not company policy.

The Procurement Agent saves the preference and confirms what it remembered.

Figure 2. Saving starts with an explicit request from the user.

 

2. Recall it in a new conversation

For project BR-JOULE-9, what preference did I ask you to remember? Recommend a supplier for 50 units of BR-MAT-100 using that preference and current supply. Include the memory ID you used.

The prompt does not repeat the five-day limit. In the live test, the agent retrieved the saved preference, returned the same memory ID, and recommended Alpha. It also recovered the same record in a new conversation after the CAP backend was redeployed.

Figure 3. Remembered context and current supply contribute different parts of the answer.

 

3. Check the second agent's access

Which Procurement preference has been explicitly shared with Fulfillment for BR-JOULE-9?

In a fresh conversation before sharing, Fulfillment reported that no preference was shared with it. The project code alone did not give it access to Procurement's private record.

 

4. Share the selected preference

Share my BR-JOULE-9 preference with Fulfillment.

Joule displayed the saved five-day preference for confirmation, with Fulfillment as the recipient and read-only access for the same signed-in user.

Figure 4. The user reviews the actual preference and confirms or cancels sharing in Joule.

I first selected Cancel, and Joule reported that access had not changed. I repeated the request and confirmed sharing. The backend then confirmed that Fulfillment had read-only access to the selected preference.

 

5. Use the memory in the handoff

In a new conversation:

Plan delivery of 50 units of BR-MAT-100 for BR-JOULE-9 using the preference explicitly shared with Fulfillment and current supply. Include the memory ID and owner. Keep the answer concise.

Fulfillment retrieved the same memory ID used by Procurement, identified Procurement as the owner, and applied the five-day limit. Its plan used current supply to recommend 50 units from Alpha with a four-day lead time.

Figure 5. A second agent uses the selected memory with read-only access, without the user repeating the preference.

The application gives Fulfillment access to the original saved record. An owner correction is available on a later retrieval without maintaining a second copy.

 

6. Revoke access

Revoke Fulfillment access to my BR-JOULE-9 preference.

I confirmed the revocation in Joule, and the backend reported success. In a new conversation, Fulfillment then reported that no preference was currently shared for the project.

Figure 6. Revoking the grant removes Fulfillment's access on a subsequent retrieval.

Revocation stops future retrieval. Text already returned in an earlier conversation remains part of that conversation, which is why this check uses a fresh one.

 

7. Check another user's boundary

For this check, the first user's read grant was active again. I signed in to Joule as a second user through SAP Cloud Identity Services and asked:

What delivery preference did I save for project BR-JOULE-9? Please check my saved memory without creating a new preference.

Procurement found no saved preference for the second user. I then asked:

What preference is available to fulfillment for project BR-JOULE-9? Check the shared memory available to me.

Fulfillment also found none. The first user's permission to reuse a memory between agents had not made it available to another person.

Figure 7. Sharing between agents preserves the boundary between signed-in users.

Finally, I asked, “Let fulfillment use my saved preference for BR-JOULE-9.” Joule could not prepare the sharing request because the second user had no owned preference for that project. Access did not change.

To check that the second account had its own usable memory, I saved a different preference for the same project: delivery within nine days, with lower cost as the priority. After sharing that record, I opened a new conversation and asked:

Can we deliver 50 units of BR-MAT-100 within the shared BR-JOULE-9 delivery limit? Use my shared preference and current offers. Include the memory ID and keep the answer concise.

Joule routed the request to Fulfillment without an agent-name prefix. It retrieved the second user's distinct memory ID and recommended Beta: eight days at EUR 70 per unit. The first user's five-day preference remained a separate record.

The application's permissions are:

Access to the planner's preferenceProcurement, same userFulfillment, same userEither agent, another user
Before sharingRead and manageNo accessNo access
After sharing the selected recordRead and manageRead onlyNo access
After revocationRead and manageNo future retrievalNo access

The signed-in owner manages sharing through Joule's confirmation step. Sharing one record leaves other preferences private.

 

Trying the pattern in another workflow

You will need SAP AI Core model access and an appropriately entitled HANA Cloud setup for Agent Memory Service. The service setup guide covers the required plans and NLP configuration. A Joule experience also requires an authenticated connection to the agents.

When adapting this example, decide what the agent should remember and how that memory should affect its work:

  1. Choose one recurring decision. Find a workflow in which users repeatedly explain the same context.
  2. Define one useful memory type. Give it an owner, a clear purpose, and a way to correct or delete it.
  3. Add one controlled handoff. Identify the second role that needs selected context and agree what it may read or change.
  4. Test the lifecycle and boundaries. Remember, recall, correct, share, revoke, and forget. Use fresh conversations and separate signed-in users. Retrieve changing business facts when making the decision.
  5. Check the resulting decision. Change a remembered constraint or a current business fact and verify that the next recommendation responds to that change. Check which memory and current data the agent used.

 

A first step toward Company Memory

Agent memory can help business agents build on earlier interactions, carry relevant context into new tasks, and collaborate without asking users to start over. Its usefulness depends on clear choices about what to retain, who can use it, and when it should be updated or forgotten. SAP HANA Cloud Agent Memory Service provides persistence and retrieval; applications put that memory to work within their own business and access rules.

We will continue exploring these topics in upcoming articles, including memory governance, collaboration between agents, and how agent memory and knowledge graphs can contribute to a broader Company Memory.

Where would memory make the biggest difference in your workflows? Share your use cases, questions, and feedback in the comments. If you found this article useful, give it a like, and let us know which topic you would like us to cover next.

entry.title: An AI agent that rebooks passengers in ABAP, and waits for your approval first
entry.content:
A flight is cancelled and nine passengers have to be moved. There are only six free seats on the alternative flights, spread over three flights and three days. Someone has to decide who goes where, and someone has to make the change in the booking system.

That is a good task for an agent, as long as the agent isn't the one who presses the button. With the September 2026 release of CAP, the agent and the approval step can both be declared in CDS. I built a small demo, Flight Rescue, to see how far that gets you against a real ABAP system:

  • A CAP-level agent (@cap-js/agents) reads the affected bookings from an ABAP Platform Trial through a custom RAP service.
  • It proposes a rebooking plan and pauses for a dispatcher to approve (@ Agent.hitl).
  • Only after approval does CAP call a RAP action that moves each booking, one at a time.
  • A SAPUI5 cockpit shows the whole flow on one screen, including a seat map that fills up as ABAP confirms each move.

The cockpit with the agent's plan waiting for approval. Each dot on the right is a seat, read from ABAP; the orange ones are the nine affected passengers.

 

What's new in the September 2026 release, and what this demo uses


FeatureStatus in the releaseUsed here for
CAP-level agents (@cap-js/agents ) : @ Agent on a CDS service gives you a ReAct loop in your CAP server, served over A2AGamma (Node.js); Java is AlphaThe rebooking agent
@ Agent.hitl: human approval before an action runsNode.js onlyApprove or reject the plan
MCP adapter: the generic describe, query (now in CQL) and call toolsGenerally availableThe agent's tools, generated from the service
Chat preview for local developmentAlpha / experimentalTesting the agent before the cockpit existed

 

Everything else is plain CAP and RAP: a remote OData V4 service, an in-memory SQLite database for the plans, and a freestyle SAPUI5 page.

 

The architecture

The ABAP side is a custom RAP business object over a Z copy of /DMO/BOOKING. It has one action, rebook, which moves a booking to another flight. The action checks everything itself: the booking still exists and isn't cancelled, it is still on the expected flight, and the target flight exists, flies the same route and has a free seat. CAP never writes to ABAP in any other way.

 

1. An agent is a CDS service with one annotation

This is the whole agent definition, apart from the system prompt:

/**
 * You are the rebooking assistant for cancelled flights. ...
 * (the doc comment is the system prompt)
 */
@agent
@agent.connect: 'none'
@requires: 'Dispatcher'
service RebookAgentService {
  @readonly entity Disruptions as projection on fr.Disruptions excluding { plans };
  @readonly entity Plans       as projection on fr.Plans excluding { agentTask };
  @readonly entity PlanItems   as projection on fr.PlanItems;

  /** The disruption, its affected bookings and the only valid alternative flights. Changes nothing. */
  function disruptionImpact(disruption : UUID) returns fr.Impact;

  /** Save a Pending rebooking plan. Nothing changes in the booking system. */
  action proposeRebooking(disruption : UUID, assignments : many fr.Assignment, rationale : String) returns fr.ProposalResult;

  /** Request human approval to run this task's Pending plan in the booking system. */
  @AGent.hitl
  action applyRebooking(plan : UUID) returns fr.ApplyResult;
}

When the server starts, the plugin does three things:

  1. It builds tools from the service: the generic MCP tools describe and query for the entities, and one tool per function or action.
  2. It runs a ReAct loop with the configured LLM.
  3. It serves the agent over A2A at /a2a/rebook-agent, plus the chat preview in development.

The LLM comes from cds.requires.llm. In this demo it points at the Anthropic model implementation that ships with the plugin, with claude-opus-5-5, because I ran everything locally. On SAP BTP you'd use the documented kind: aicore instead, which goes through SAP AI Core and is the default in the production and hybrid profiles. In development, the default kind: auto picks up the credentials of a local Claude Code or OpenCode installation, so you may not need any configuration at all.

@requires: 'Dispatcher' works as it does on any CAP service: a user without the role can't talk to the agent at all.

What I like most here is that the agent can read only the three projections and call the three operations. It has no SQL connection, no generic HTTP client and no ABAP credentials. If something isn't in the service, the agent can't do it.

Two notes on the annotations:

  • @ Agent.connect: 'none' keeps the agent narrow: no extra MCP servers, no subagents. The plugin reads this annotation, but at the time of writing it isn't in the capire guide, so check that it still exists before you rely on it.
  • I included no AGENTS.md, on purpose. The release also lets you put an AGENTS.md and skills/*/SKILL.md files next to the service. When AGENTS.md is present, the plugin builds the agent from that directory instead of the generic ReAct agent. That is the right choice for a rich assistant like the XTravels sample. For a single, narrow job, the service's doc comment as the system prompt was enough.

 

2. The model sees CQL, not OData

The MCP adapter is generally available (GA) in this release, and its query tool now takes CQL. In the server log you can watch the agent work it out: it describes the entity, queries it, and then calls the custom functions:

[agents] - RebookAgentService request { method: 'message/send', text: 'LH 0402 on 2026-12-31 is cancelled. Rebook the passengers.' }
[mcp] - RebookAgentService describe { entities: [ 'Disruptions' ] }
[mcp] - RebookAgentService query {
  cql: "SELECT ID, carrierId, connectionId, flightDate, airportFrom, airportTo, reason, status FROM Disruptions
        WHERE carrierId = 'LH' AND connectionId = '0402' AND flightDate = '2026-12-31'"
}
[mcp] - RebookAgentService - call disruptionImpact { disruption: '4538ad9d-…' }
[mcp] - RebookAgentService - call proposeRebooking { disruption: '4538ad9d-…', assignments: [ … ] }

This log is unedited apart from line breaks. I didn't write any tool code for describe or query.

 

What the ReAct loop is doing here

ReAct stands for "Reasoning and Acting": the model works in rounds. In each round it reads the conversation so far and either asks for a tool call or writes its final answer. The server runs the tool, adds the result to the conversation, and the next round starts. The model never executes anything itself. It only asks, and CAP decides.

The loop runs inside the CAP server. The plugin builds it with LangGraph and keeps the conversation and checkpoints in CAP's database. In every round the model gets the same three things:

  • the system prompt, which is the service's doc comment
  • the five tools generated from the service
  • the conversation so far, including every earlier tool result

The log above, round by round:

     
RoundThe model asks forWhat CAP does
1describe DisruptionsReturns the entity's fields
2query with a CQL SELECT … FROM Disruptions WHERE …Runs it on the service, with the dispatcher's authorisations
3disruptionImpactMy handler reads the bookings from ABAP and returns the 9 bookings and the only valid alternatives
4proposeRebookingMy handler checks the plan against the rules and saves it as Pending
5applyRebookingDoesn't run it. The loop stops here and waits for a human (next section)
6after ApproveRuns the action, which moves the bookings in ABAP
7the final answerShows the summary in the chat

 

The model decides the order of the calls, so two runs can take different paths and produce different plans. What it may call is fixed, though. There are only five tools, and each one goes through ordinary CAP handlers and @requires checks.

 

3. @ Agent.hitl: the pause

Here is the part that makes this usable for something that changes business data. Because applyRebooking is annotated @ Agent.hitl, the action doesn't run when the model decides to call it. Instead, the A2A task goes to the input-required state, and the pending call (including the plan ID) is in the task's status message:

task.status.state                                   // 'input-required'
task.status.message.metadata['sap.cds.agents.hitl']
    .actionRequests[0].args.plan                    // the plan waiting for approval

Any A2A client can then resume the same task with an approval or a rejection. In the cockpit, those are two JSON-RPC message/send calls:

approve: task => send([{ kind: 'text', text: 'approve' }], task),
reject: (task, message) => send([{ kind: 'data', data: { decisions: [{ type: 'reject', message }] } }], task)

send adds the task's taskId and contextId.

Prompts aren't a good control, but this is. The system prompt does tell the model not to ask for confirmation in text, but the guarantee doesn't depend on the model following it. Whatever the model writes, the action body doesn't run until a human resumes the task. With audit logging set up (I didn't in this demo), the plugin also records each approval or rejection as an AgentTaskResumed event.

I only had to put a UI on top. The cockpit shows the paused plan as a card with Approve and Reject, grouped by target flight, with the number of unassigned passengers and the agent's reasoning.

The paused task as the dispatcher sees it. The reasoning is the model's own; the numbers come from the server.

 

4. Approval

The domain rules are ordinary CAP code, and the agent can only choose among options the server has already checked:

  • disruptionImpact returns the affected bookings and the only valid alternatives: same route, same day up to two days later, seats left after other pending plans.
  • proposeRebooking refuses any booking, flight or seat count outside that list. It saves a Pending plan and changes nothing in ABAP.
  • The plan is bound to its agent task. The A2A task ID travels server-side, so it is never a tool argument. A resumed call that points at a different plan is refused (NOT_REVIEWED).
  • Each booking is moved with its expected current flight. If someone changed the booking in ABAP after the proposal, that one fails alone (STALE), and the rest still apply.
  • The model sees no customer data, only travel and booking IDs, flights and seat counts.

Because the agent is a CAP service, I could also tighten the generated tools with a normal CAP handler. The plugin raises a buildTools event, so a few lines check the tool list against an allowlist at startup and make the tool schemas strict, so unknown arguments are refused rather than dropped:

this.on('buildTools', async (req, next) => {
  const tools = await next()
  if (tools.map(t => t.name).join() !== TOOLS.join()) throw new Error('Agent tools differ from the allowlist')
  for (const t of tools) if (OPERATIONS.includes(t.name)) t.schema = t.schema.strict()
  return tools
})

 

5. Run against a real ABAP system

The agent's data access goes through one CAP remote service, ZFR_REBOOK. Its CDS model matches the $metadata of the published OData V4 binding.

  • Without credentials: cds watch mocks the service from the same contract. The mock applies the same checks and messages as the ABAP action, so the whole flow runs offline. The tests use a scripted model, so they need no API key either.
  • With credentials: set ABAP_URL, SAP_USER and SAP_PASSWORD as environment variables, and the same code talks to the ABAP Platform Trial.

In the run I recorded, the scenario was LH 0402 on FRA–EWR, with 9 bookings in three travels and 6 free seats on five alternatives. The agent proposed the following, and left 3 bookings unassigned with a reason:

  • travel 90000003 (2 bookings) → UA 0043, same day
  • travel 90000002 (3 bookings) → LH 0402, the next day
  • one booking of travel 90000001 → UA 0043, the next day

The plan isn't scripted. In the take shown in the GIF at the top, the agent split travel 90000001 across two flights and left travel 90000002 unassigned instead. Both plans stay within the seats the server listed, and that's the point: the model chooses, the server decides what it may choose from.

After Approve, the table in ABAP showed exactly those six moves, and the three alternatives were full. A Reject on a fresh scenario left all nine bookings where they were.

Before: the disruption is declared and nobody has moved yet.

After Approve: six orange seats have moved to the alternatives, which are now full, and three passengers are still on the cancelled flight. The agent's summary is in the chat.

 

Lessons learned

  • The A2A endpoint and browser logins. With mocked or basic authentication, the A2A endpoint answers 401 without a WWW-Authenticate challenge, so a browser never sends it the login it already uses for the OData service. A three-line middleware that adds the Basic challenge fixed it for local development. A deployed app with tokens doesn't need it.
  • RAP and leading zeros. The OData V4 binding returns NUMC fields without leading zeros ("TravelId":"4506") but accepts them with. I pad them in the one module that talks to ABAP.
  • Messages from RAP are cut at 50 characters when created with new_message_with_text, so keep the action's texts short. They end up in front of the dispatcher, and in front of the model.

 

A word on the SAP API Policy

The CAP documentation is explicit: CAP-level agents are meant for exposing custom CAP application services. They are not an SAP-endorsed pathway for agentic access to SAP Application APIs (section 2.2.2 of the SAP API Policy). This demo stays inside that line. The agent exposes only this app's own services, and the ABAP side is a custom Z RAP service over custom tables. For agentic access to SAP Application APIs, the CAP docs point to the reference architectures in the SAP Architecture Center.

 

Try it yourself

  • Code: https://github.com/Kamilkov/flight-rescue.git 
  • CAP release notes, September 2026: https://cap.cloud.sap/docs/releases/2026/sep26
  • CAP-level agents guide: https://cap.cloud.sap/docs/guides/ai/cap-agents
  • MCP adapter guide: https://cap.cloud.sap/docs/guides/ai/cap-mcp

entry.title: AI had one set of instructions and broke it fearlessly — then apologised!
entry.content:
Hi. I'm Andréa Molina, an SAP engineer with 20+ years of experience, working hands-on with BTP, UX, and AI. 

I shared my  An Engineering Manifesto for AI-Assisted SAP Development — Let's Build It Together blog with 19 principles, examples and code patterns for SAP Development yesterday.

And on the very first real test AI broke the instructions!  😬

What happened

I was testing an OData service for a CAP app. AI suggested I hardcode my password in the package.json. The manifesto said, in plain words, never to do that.

When I called it out, it replied:

As funny as it is, this is serious. Very serious!

The AI could explain perfectly why the action was wrong but only after it had already proposed doing it.

What if I hadn’t reviewed the code before shipping it?
What if those credentials had travelled somewhere they shouldn’t?

A code agent recently deleted a company's entire database in nine seconds, trying to 'fix' a credential problem!  Then it wrote an apology listing the safety rules it had broken!  Sounds familiar?

Luckily I am always concerned about quality, security and governance and stopped it straight away. What if it was a new IT person with not much experience to understand that it's a security breach? What if it was a person building  an app with no IT training that was just following AIs instructions?

Why a human HAS to stay in the loop

AI has no skin in the game. If it breaches security, it won't lose its job or its reputation. It apologises and moves on. 

And there’s a quieter risk: the more we use AI, the more we trust it. Our guard drops — slowly, quietly.

A friend once ended a debate with "but AI said so". I am sorry. NO. AI is a co-worker, a very capable one, but still just a co-worker.

I am definitely not against AI. I use it daily, to prepare for meetings, code, structure discussions, help with questions, to learn about the new SAP world, to help me create my study plan and we argue a lot hahaha. But when I am using it for code I read every line before shipping and I always search for the information until I am comfortable with it. 

If I find something important, it goes straight into the manifesto.

The fix (we will see that ahahah)

I added this to the manifesto and updated the original post:

"If a scenario requires credentials or tokens to function, stop, do not suggest any workaround, and ask the user to define the secure pattern before proceeding."

A lesson about rules for AI

Writing rules for AI means making implicit expectations explicit. What seems obvious to a human engineer may not be a reliable constraint for an AI system.

We’re still years away from fully maturing:

  • how we give instructions,

  • how we build agents that don’t override them,

  • how we remove bias from our data.

Human-in-the-loop is not optional. It’s mandatory, and will remain so.

Talking about bias and human-in-the-loop being important : Amazon ditched AI recruiting tool that favored men for technical jobs

And here's the ironic part: none of this is new. While we talk about this as novelty, Human in the loop, ownership, continuous improvement, the ironies of automation are discussed for decades. Soon I'll write a new blog about what Toyota has to do with all this.

Your turn

Have you ever run into AI breaking a rule you gave it? Or has it ever asked you to do something so crazy it hurts?

entry.title: What a side project taught me about S/4HANA finance data (CAP + freestyle UI5)
entry.content:
I'm a BTP developer, not a finance person. But one thing I keep seeing at companies on S/4HANA is this: budget owners never log into SAP. Every month the controller exports a cost center report to Excel, emails it out, and then the questions start coming back.

Problem

What bothered me about that loop:

  • Managers get a report full of G/L accounts. They don't know what those are, and they shouldn't have to.
  • It shows what's spent, but not what's already ordered. So the "left to spend" number is basically wrong.
  • The controller answers the same kind of questions by email, every single month.

I wanted to see if a small side-by-side app could fix that, and honestly, to learn how finance data in S/4HANA really works. So I built a prototype in my spare time, on fake data shaped like the real S/4HANA APIs. Here's what I learned along the way.

1. Managers ask "Am I OK?", not "What's on this G/L account?"

Managers don't care about G/L accounts. They just want to know if they're OK. So every page starts with one sentence that answers that, like "You're $81.4K over plan so far this year, mostly from one $86.5K invoice in July."

Open POs turned out to matter just as much. If you don't subtract what's already ordered, "left to spend" doesn't mean much. So the page shows three numbers: spent, already ordered (open POs) and what's left.

2. Let code do the math, not the AI

This is my one hard rule. All the numbers come from plain code with unit tests, and the sentences get built from those numbers after. If I ever add an LLM, it only gets to rephrase. Never calculate. One wrong number and finance people stop trusting the whole thing.

The same math also does a what-if: if I buy this, where do I end up at year-end?

3. Clean core means the app's own data stays on BTP

The app only reads from S/4HANA (on-prem / Private Edition 2023+), and only through released APIs. This part taught me the most. For actuals I first went with the Journal Entry Item - Read API. Then I read its help page: it's meant for SAP Analytics Cloud only. So I switched to G/L Account Line Items - Read (API_GLACCOUNTLINEITEM), which has cost centers, suppliers and POs. Lesson learned: read the restrictions, not just the field list.

Open orders come from the Purchase Order API, minus whatever's already been posted against each PO. For plan data I found Financial Planning Entry Item - Read (ACDOCP). Not sure yet if that's how customers really plan, so that's my first question below.

Anything managers create, like comments and "this isn't my cost" requests, lives in the app on BTP. The controller still posts the reclass in S/4HANA, so nothing gets written back to the core.

 

4. Test your mock data like code

My fake data comes from a Node.js script. While taking these screenshots I caught a bug: a manager disputed an invoice two days before it was even posted. The posting date was generated, but I'd hardcoded the comment dates.

Now the comment dates are based on the posting date, and the script fails if a comment ever comes before its invoice. A controller would spot that in a second, and then they'd doubt every other number too.

 

Conclusion

Honestly, the code was the easy part. The hard part was learning to look at finance data the way a manager does, and making sure every number traces back to the ledger.

Questions for the community

I'm still learning the finance side, so I'd really appreciate input from anyone who works with S/4HANA FI/CO:

  1. For plan data I found Financial Planning Entry Item - Read (ACDOCP). Is that what you'd use, or do customers still keep cost center plans in the classic CO tables?
  2. How do you present commitments to non-finance users?
  3. What have I got wrong about how controllers and budget owners work together?

All screenshots use fictional companies and people.

entry.title: SAP Developer tools are available on Open VSX Registry
entry.content:
SAP Developer Tools Are Now on Open VSX Registry!

 

Why That Matters

Developers don’t all work in the same editor. Some live in Visual Studio Code or VS Code. Some use Eclipse Theia-based environments in the cloud. And a growing number run AI-native editors where VS Code compatibility is the baseline — but the Microsoft Marketplace is not.

This isn’t a niche edge case. The VS Code-compatible editor ecosystem has expanded significantly, and Microsoft’s extension marketplace is not accessible from most of them. For SAP developers working in those environments, that has historically meant missing out on the tooling they need to build SAP applications effectively.

We hope that this changes with SAP’s publication on Open VSX (open-vsx.org/namespace/SAPSE).

What Is Open VSX Registry?

Open VSX is a vendor-neutral extension registry operated by the Eclipse Foundation. It is the standard distribution channel for VS Code extensions in any editor that does not have direct access to the Microsoft Marketplace — which covers a wide and growing set of environments used by professional developers today.

 

Where the Microsoft Marketplace is tied to the Microsoft ecosystem, Open VSX is open infrastructure. Any VS Code-compatible editor can consume it. Any publisher can list extensions without vendor agreements. It is how the broader editor ecosystem accesses the extension tooling it needs.

SAP’s Developer Strategy: Choice Without Compromise

SAP’s position is straightforward: developers should be able to work in the environment that makes them most productive. The SAP tooling needed to build cloud applications, Fiori UIs, and mobile solutions should follow them there — not require them to switch editors.

 

Publishing on Open VSX is how SAP delivers on that. It ensures that SAP’s developer extensions are available wherever VS Code-compatible editors are used, without requiring developers to compromise on their setup.

This is the direct continuation of the work announced in this VS Code extensions blog.

What’s Published Under the SAPSE Namespace

The following eight extensions are available today at open-vsx.org/namespace/SAPSE:

SAP CDS Language Support

Language support for SAP Core Data Services delivers syntax highlighting, Language Server Protocol integration, real-time diagnostics, and formatting for .cds files. The foundational extension for SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP) development — if you’re building CAP services, this is where you start.

Core Data Services Graphical Modeler

CDS Graphical Modeler allows the developer to model CDS files in SAP Cloud Application Programming model development projects and enables increased productivity in designing CDS model via the graphical editor. Both CAP (.cds) and ABAP CDS (.csn) files can be edited.

SAP Fiori Tools — Extension Pack

A bundled pack that installs the full SAP Fiori development toolchain in one step. The recommended starting point for any Fiori Elements or SAPUI5 project.

SAP Fiori Tools — Application Modeler

A visual representation of a Fiori application’s page structure, navigation targets, and service entities. The Page Map view lets you add navigation, manage pages, and modify application structure directly — no manual configuration file editing required.

SAP Fiori Tools — XML Annotation Language Server

Authoring support for OData annotations — the metadata layer that drives how Fiori Elements applications render and behave. Provides code completion, micro-snippets, i18n support, and real-time diagnostics as you write annotation files.

SAP Fiori Tools — Service Modeler

A combined view of an OData service and its associated annotations helping to understand a service’s structure and annotation coverage without parsing raw metadata — particularly when connecting Fiori applications to SAP backend systems.

SAP Fiori Tools — Guided Development

In-editor access to how-to guides and step-by-step tutorials for implementing Fiori Elements features. Contextual guidance surfaces during development, so the relevant SAP documentation is available without leaving the editor.

Mobile Development Kit Editor

Visual development tools for the mobile development kit, SAP's platform for building enterprise-grade cross-platform mobile applications with offline capabilities, OData backend synchronization, and deployment across iOS and Android. The end-to-end development capabilities includes visual editing, debugging support, and code snippets, enabling developers to build, debug, and maintain mobile applications directly within the IDE.

Getting Started

If you’re working in a Visual Studio Code-compatible editor, search for SAPSE in your extension marketplace — or navigate directly to open-vsx.org/namespace/SAPSE. 

While Visual Studio Code users can continue using the Microsoft Marketplace/SAP SE as before. Open VSX serves developers who work in other growing ecosystem of editors built on VS Code’s foundations.

The extensions are the same. The tooling is the same. The only difference is that more developers can now use it — in the editor they choose.

Follow SAP Application Development on the SAP Community for updates on developer tooling, CAP, Fiori development, and mobile.

entry.title: GeoTrack: tracking trips in SAP HANA Cloud
entry.content:
GeoTrack is a portfolio project with exactly one user: me.

  • My iPhone records where I go.
  • My Apple Watch records my walks and hikes, and I pick the photos I want to keep.
  • Everything lands in SAP HANA Cloud.
  • Its spatial engine, which lets SQL store and measure points, lines and areas, turns raw positions into zones, trips and routes.
  • A RAP business object on an ABAP system records my visits to selected places.
  • A Fiori Elements app shows each trip with its route on a map, my heart rate, the altitude profile, the photos and the weather of every hour.
  • Claude, Anthropic's AI model, can answer questions about my trips through MCP tools.

I did not write GeoTrack's code. I decided what it should do and approved each design, and Claude wrote the code and the tests in Claude Code, from the HANA model and the RAP object to the Fiori app and the iOS app. I ran it on my own server and phone and checked the results.

This post walks through both versions of the architecture, explains why I asked Claude to replace two off-the-shelf senders with one iOS app, and shows the HANA spatial SQL that does the actual work.

The coordinates in the SQL examples are made up. The screenshots show real trips.

 

What GeoTrack does

  • Positions. Every position from the phone is stored as an ST_POINT in HANA Cloud, also while the trial database sleeps at night.
  • Zones. Places such as home, the supermarket or a trailhead are circles or polygons. A position inside a private zone is coarsened to the zone's centre before it is written.
  • Trips. Positions are cut into walks and drives using the iOS motion activity, and each route is stored as a LINESTRING.
  • Visits. A confirmed stay in a selected zone becomes a SiteVisit, a RAP business object on an ABAP Platform trial system.
  • Weather. Every closed trip gets the hourly weather from Open-Meteo.
  • Workouts and photos. Apple Watch workouts (always hikes - I live in the mountains), with heart rate and GPS route, and my photos are linked to the trips they belong to.
  • Apps. A read-only Fiori Elements List Report and Object Page shows all of it, and MCP tools let Claude answer questions about it.

 

Version 1: three senders

The first version used the best existing app for each job.

Positions came from OwnTracks. In Move mode it publishes a position when I have moved 50 m or when 300 seconds have passed. It sent JSON over MQTT to a Mosquitto broker on my VPS. The CAP service subscribed and acknowledged a message only after HANA had committed it.

Workouts came from Health Auto Export. Its REST automation posted my Apple Watch workouts, with heart rate samples and the GPS route, to an endpoint of the CAP service. It synced about once an hour after I unlocked the phone.
