entry.title: AI Agents: Join fan-out, overlapping totals and a custom measure service in SAP CAP
entry.content:
• You ask an AI Agent a business question,
  • he writes SQL that joins a few tables,
  • the joins repeat rows,
  • SUM happily adds up the repeats.

The answer comes back confident, nicely formatted and also wrong.

The idea came from a video by Google Cloud Tech: BigQuery Graph measures explained (Why your AI agents get metrics wrong and how measures fix it) 

I hadn't personally noticed this problem before, so I was curious whether I could reproduce it, and whether the model or the tools made the bigger difference.

Claude Code suggested we might turn it into an eval. We chose the following three models as the guinea pigs:

  1. gemini-3.8-flash
  2. gemini-3.5-flash-lite, the smallest current Gemini with function calling
  3. Gemma 4 26B-A4B — Google's open-weight mixture-of-experts model, with about 4 billion parameters active per token. The kind of model people run on their own hardware. In this case I ran it hosted on the Gemini API, so this isn't a test of local or quantised inference.

 

Setting the trap

The playground is Chinook, the music store sample database that half the internet learned SQL on (MIT licence).

  • Tracks,
  • albums,
  • artists,
  • playlists,
  • invoices,
  • invoice lines.

To really set the trap, Claude added some clearly labelled synthetic data:

  • streams per track (very uneven, with a dozen famous hits on top)
  • 20 "editorial" playlists which, like real ones, can't get enough of the popular tracks.

Now ask: "How many streams do the tracks on our editorial playlists have in total?"

The obvious SQL joins Tracks to PlaylistTracks to Playlists and sums the streams. 'Bohemian Rhapsody' sits on 8 editorial playlists, so its streams get counted 8 times. The answer comes out as 30.7 billion. The correct one is 5.08 billion. Six times too much, and nothing in the result looks the least bit suspicious.

We ABAPers know this one by heart: it's the header amount from VBAK summed once per item in VBAP. Chinook has it too. "What is the total invoiced amount of the invoices that include at least one 'Rock' track?" Join the invoices to their lines to filter on the genre, sum the invoice total, and you get 7,720.02 instead of 1,639.03.

The nastiest one is the grand total. "Show streams per editorial playlist, with a grand total." Every per-playlist number is correct. Add them up, though, and you get 30.7 billion again, because the playlists overlap. Count each qualifying track once and you get 5.08 billion. Both numbers describe something, but they answer different questions. For this demo, I defined the grand total as the second one.

In the end Claude Opus 5.5 wrote 8 such questions, each with its correct answer and the "naive" answer the joins give. Those became the golden answers everything else gets measured against, and that's how I ended up running my first ever eval.

 

Measures

The solution that Google's video proposes is Measures.

What is a measure? Think of a company where people work on several project teams at once. "How many people work on projects?" You can't just add up the team sizes: Anna is on three teams, so she'd be counted three times. Instead you go through the staff list once and tick everyone who is on at least one team. That's a measure: a number defined once, on the table it belongs to (headcount lives on the staff list), and counted there, once per person. Other tables only decide who gets ticked. They never get to count anybody twice.

Here, streams live on tracks. "Streams on editorial playlists" means: go through the tracks once and add up every track that sits on at least one editorial playlist. 'Bohemian Rhapsody' counts once, not 8 times. Ask for streams per playlist, and every row is right, but the rows don't add up to the total, because the playlists overlap. The measure knows that and hands you the distinct-track total separately. And the Agent doesn't write any SQL at all: he just asks for "streams" by name.

 

Measures in CAP

For this demo, I had a small custom measure service built on SAP CAP (@ SAP/cds 10.1.1 on SQLite). It applies the same idea using CAP's CQL exists predicates; it isn't a built-in CAP measure engine. About 320 lines, with every measure counted on its home entity:

streams:        { entity: 'Tracks',       expr: 'sum(streams)' },
revenue:        { entity: 'InvoiceLines', expr: 'round(sum(unitPrice * quantity), 2)' },
invoicedAmount: { entity: 'Invoices',     expr: 'round(sum(total), 2)' },
followers:      { entity: 'Playlists',    expr: 'sum(followers)' },
artists:        { entity: 'Artists',      expr: 'count(*)' },

The important bit is the shape of the query: aggregate the home entity, and use EXISTS to decide which rows qualify. The related rows filter the total; they don't multiply it. ( https://cap.cloud.sap/docs/cds/cql#exists-predicate )

All other entities can only filter a measure, through CQL exists, and nothing ever joins along a to-many association. The Agent doesn't write SQL at all. He sends a request like this:

{ "measures": ["streams"], "groupBy": "Playlists.name",
  "filters": [{ "field": "Playlists.editorial", "op": "=", "value": true }] }

... and gets back 20 rows, plus "additive": false and "total": { "streams": 5075440217 }. In plain words: these groups overlap, don't add them up, here's the distinct-track total.

 

The experiment: So much for my headline

Then finally the experiment:

  • Two Agents per Model, same question, same definitions of what each number means.
  • Agent A gets the table definitions and writes raw SQL against a read-only copy of the database.
  • Agent B gets only the measure tool.
  • Each can make up to 8 tool calls per question.
  • Each answers the 8 questions 5 times, and a script scores every answer against the golden ones. It also checks whether a wrong answer is exactly the naive one, so a double-count can't hide among the ordinary mistakes.

There is a difference worth spelling out. Agent B also gets instructions explaining additive and total, and the tool calculates the distinct-track total for it. Agent A gets the measure definitions, but no equally explicit instruction about overlapping grand totals. So this compares two agent setups, including their tools and instructions. It doesn't isolate SQL-writing ability alone.

First run, with gemini-3.8-flash:

  • Agent A gave the correct answer 35 times out of 40,
  • Agent B 40 out of 40.

Is that the "AI double-counts" story I was hoping for? Not really. The Model dodged the join traps with IN (subquery) like a seasoned pro. All 5 of its misses were the grand total. In 3 of those 5 runs it actually computed the distinct-track total along the way. In run 5 its last statement returned 5,075,440,217, and then it reported 30,734,635,048 anyway.

So I wrote down every remaining condition in the spec, and carried out the second run:

  • The raw SQL agent writes its own SQL.
  • The measure agent only asks for measures by name.
  • The "definitions" are a short glossary in the prompt saying what each number means, for example streams: sum(streams) over chinook_Tracks.

 

Gemini 3.5-flash-lite

The 3.5-flash-lite walks into every trap. With the definitions, 22 of its 29 misses are exactly the number the naive join gives. On the streams question it wrote one plain join, five runs out of five. On the 'Rock' invoices it tried to be clever about the duplicates:

SELECT sum(DISTINCT i.total) AS value
FROM chinook_Invoices i
JOIN chinook_InvoiceLines il ON i.ID = il.invoice_ID
JOIN chinook_Tracks t ON il.track_ID = t.ID
JOIN chinook_Genres g ON t.genre_ID = g.ID
WHERE g.name = 'Rock'

SUM(DISTINCT) also merges different invoices that happen to have the same amount, so the answer was 166.74 instead of 1,639.03. Nice try, though.

Give the same small Model the measure tool and it gets 39 of 40. The one miss forgot the Rock filter.

 

Gemma-4

Gemma's first attempt didn't make it past run 1. 4 of 7 measure answers failed the format check, although every one of them ended in perfectly valid JSON. Turns out Gemma sends its reasoning along as separate "thought" parts, and the harness glued them in front of the answer.

On top of that, the Gemma endpoint I used was limited to 16,000 input tokens per minute, and the harness gave up on the 429s far too early. Neither had anything to do with measures, and the score alone would have said Gemma can't write JSON. So I stopped the run, fixed the harness, set those results aside and started again from scratch.

Second attempt, all the way through. With raw SQL, Gemma got 34 of 40, and 31 without the definitions: about as good as gemini-3.8-flash. Across the two raw-SQL conditions, all 15 misses matched the naive totals; 10 were the grand total. With measures: 34 of 40. Exactly the same. Do measures do nothing for Gemma, then? Not quite.

Reading the failed runs told a different story. With measures, Gemma double-counted only once: it added up the playlist rows, although the tool had just told it they overlap. The rest had nothing to do with double-counting. Gemma writes the filter value as "True", with a capital T. The tool only understood a lowercase "true", so the filter matched nothing, and the tool cheerfully reported 0 followers. No error, nothing.

Gemma sent "True" in 9 of its 40 runs and recovered 8 times. The ninth time it answered 0. Three more runs on the 'Nirvana' question ran out of turns without an answer, and the harness had thrown their calls away, so I couldn't even see why. And once Gemma had the right 'Rock' invoice total after three calls, didn't trust it, used up all 8 and never gave a proper answer.

So the bug was in the tool. The fix was easy: any spelling of true or false now works, anything else gets an error instead of a silent zero, and the harness keeps the calls of a run that never answers.

Follow-up, measures only: 36 of 40, and not a single double-count. All 4 misses came from one habit: Gemma spells out the path, as in Playlists.tracks.artists.name, where the tool wants Artists.name and finds the path by itself. "Unknown entity", a few more tries, and then three times a confident wrong number on the 'Nirvana' question (1.6, 3.8 and 66.1 million followers instead of 72.4 million), and once no answer at all on the 'Rock' invoices.

 

Making it visible

Numbers in a JSON file don't make much of a demo, so next came a UI: SAPUI5 1.136.8 served straight from CAP, with the NetworkGraph from sap.suite.ui.commons. It opens with the scoreboard, then the totals view: one bar per editorial playlist, the sum of the bars, and the distinct-track total, all on one scale. Next to it, a graph of the top 10 tracks and the playlists they sit on. Click 'Bohemian Rhapsody' and it tells you its streams get counted 8 times. Every SQL statement the Agents wrote can be replayed against the database with one click.

 

Measures via MCP

The last project slice puts the measure tool behind MCP, with @cap-js/mcp 1.5.0. Two tools:

  • catalog (what you can measure, filter and group by).
  • aggregate.

Claude ran a headless Claude Code on Haiku 5.5, from an empty folder, with no tools at all except this MCP server, and asked the grand total question. Haiku called catalog, then aggregate, answered with the correct 5.08 billion, and added on his own that the rows don't add up to the total because a track can sit on several playlists. Cost: about a third of a cent. One run, so an anecdote rather than an eval, but a nice one.

 

How does it all add up

So, did these Agents double-count? Yes. Flash-Lite often fell into the join traps. Flash usually avoided them, but all five misses with definitions were the overlapping grand total. Gemma's raw-SQL misses also matched the naive totals. That's what happened on these eight questions; I wouldn't turn it into a rule about small and big Models.

What I take away is three things, in this order.

  1. On these questions, measures helped the small Model a lot: 11 of 40 with raw SQL and definitions, 39 of 40 with measures. Same Model, different tools. And when groups overlap, somebody still has to decide what “total” means. Here, that decision lives in the measure service.
  2. This makes me curious about locally-run Models. Gemma wrote SQL about as well as Flash in this demo, but still sometimes struggled with the measure tool. I ran it hosted, though. Whether the same holds on my Mac, or with a quantised copy, is a separate experiment.
  3. Read the failures, not just the scores. The scores said Gemma can't write JSON and gets nothing out of measures. The failed runs said: two faults in the harness, a bug in the tool, and a Model that likes to spell out its paths. None of that shows up in a number.

What's an eval, anyway? A fixed set of questions with known right answers, put to a Model (or an Agent) again and again and scored by a script rather than by eyeballing, so you can compare one setup with another and trust the difference. Strictly speaking, this one ticks those boxes, but only just. 8 questions are far too few to generalise from. They were written to contain the trap, not picked from real use. The same Claude that designed the measure tool also wrote the questions. And with 5 runs per question, a difference of 2 or 3 answers out of 40 could be plain luck. So: a demo with an eval's discipline, not a benchmark.

  • 8 questions, 5 runs each.
  • Only Google Models (two Gemini, one Gemma)
  • Gemma ran hosted, not on my Mac.
  • Streams, editorial playlists and followers are synthetic; everything else is Chinook.
  • I haven't tried it on HANA Cloud yet.
  • The code, the golden answers and every recorded run, with every SQL statement the Agents wrote, are on GitHub: github.com/Kamilkov/graph-measures.

 

P.S.: My setup: a Mac, Node 26, @ SAP/cds 10.1.1 with SQLite, SAPUI5 1.136.8, @cap-js/mcp 1.5.0. Gemini 3.8 Flash wrote the code, Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code reviewed it, and both Agents in the eval called the Gemini API. This post was assisted by GenAI.

entry.title: A Battery Recall, a Graph, and an AI Agent
entry.content:
This is a personal portfolio project exploring graph capabilities of the SAP HANA database. It tries to answer two questions: can a graph find everyone affected by a motorcycle battery recall, and can an AI Agent make a sensible remedy plan when replacement battery packs are scarce.

 

I asked Claude Code (Opus 5.5) what would be a good showcase for a graph. He suggested we do a spike first: a quick, throwaway experiment to see whether an idea holds water before anyone builds anything.

 

Spike one: The where-used index

The first candidate was ABAP's own where-used index. Table WBCROSSGT has 9.7 million rows on my A4H, and as a graph of who uses which type it came to 205,145 vertices and 1,017,224 edges. Unknown depth, cycles, the lot. Surely a job for a graph?

Turns out, not really. A plain ABAP loop of about 25 lines (level by level, SELECT ... FOR ALL ENTRIES, a hashed table of what it had already seen) found exactly the same objects in all four test cases, within about 2 seconds and with no setup. Warm, the graph was 3 to 8 times faster, but building it cold took 7 to 14 seconds. And the one job that should have been its home turf, finding cycles, gave no answer after 9 minutes, so we aborted it.

So much for that.

 

Spike two: The real-life project

Then I remembered a project I once did.

  • A manufacturing component is found to be defective.
  • Find all production orders where it was used,
  • then find the subsequent production orders where the material produced in the previous one was used as a component (several levels deep),
  • then find the sales orders where it was sold,
  • then find out whether it was shipped to a customer or is still at a storage location.

The objective: notify the customer and send them a replacement, or take the product out of the storage location and scrap it.

Would that have been a good case for a graph? We had no data to try it on. So we invented some, and gave it a home in my Supply Chain Rescue demo app, which already has a fictional maker of electric motorcycles. Electric motorcycles have batteries. Batteries have cell lots. You can see where this is going.

A second spike on that idea went better, so we built the real thing: Recall Rescue.

 

The battery genealogy

Claude generated 12 weeks of motorcycle production and sales, from week 28 of 2026, with a battery genealogy behind every one of them:

  • a cell lot from the supplier VoltCell goes into battery modules,
  • modules go into packs,
  • packs go into motorcycles, or wait at the service stock as spare packs,
  • motorcycles go to customers, or wait at a plant, a dealer or the service stock.

That alone would be a tree: every module sits in one pack and every pack in one motorcycle, so from any module there is exactly one way forward. What breaks the simple tree is reuse and remanufacturing:

  • On 1 September, 8 private motorcycles from week 29 got a new pack.
  • Their old packs were taken apart, and 2 modules each from 2 old packs made one remanufactured pack.

So now a module has two links:

  1. the old one to the pack it came from,
  2. the new one to the remanufactured pack.

On 21 September, 3 of the remanufactured packs went into motorcycles sold in weeks 31 to 35, under warranty. The old links stay in the database as history, marked inactive, and that will matter in a minute.

A perfect setup to declare one lot defective and try to trace it.

Side note: the EU thinks along the same lines. From 18 February 2027 every LMT and electric vehicle battery placed on the EU market, electric motorcycle batteries included, needs a battery passport, and a remanufactured battery gets "a new battery passport linked to the battery passport or passports of the original battery or batteries" (Article 77 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542). Recall Rescue doesn't build passports, mind you, but the links behind them make a graph for the same reason the workshop does here.

 

All in all 27,814 items and 42,487 links in two Database Tables in A4H, generated from a fixed seed, so the world comes out the same every time.

 

Four lines of openCypher

If you haven't met openCypher yet: it's a query language for graphs, the open version of Cypher, which came from Neo4j. Where SQL makes you join tables, openCypher has you draw the pattern you're looking for, in ASCII art. (a) is a node, -[r]-> is a relationship pointing from one node to the next, and [*1..4] means 1 to 4 relationships, whatever lies in between (the part that takes a loop in ABAP).

  • MATCH draws the pattern,
  • WHERE filters it,
  • RETURN says what you want back.

HANA understands a subset of it and runs it against a graph workspace.

The question for a recall is: who has a battery with cells from this lot, right now? In openCypher it reads almost like the sentence (RETURN trimmed):

MATCH p = (l)-[*1..4]->(u), (u)-[h]->(t)
WHERE l.VERTEXID = 'LOT-VC-W29-03' AND (u.KIND = 'VIN' OR u.KIND = 'PACK') AND (t.KIND = 'CUST' OR t.KIND = 'SLOC')
  AND h.ACTIVE = 'X' AND ALL(e IN RELATIONSHIPS(p) WHERE e.ACTIVE = 'X')
RETURN u.VERTEXID AS UNIT, t.VERTEXID AS HOLDER

Start at the lot, follow 1 to 4 links to a motorcycle or a pack, then one more link to whoever holds it - a customer or a storage location. Current links only.

That last condition is important. For the lot LOT-VC-W29-03 the trace finds 27 units with their holders. Let it follow the history too, and it finds 35: Eight customers would get a recall notice for a battery that isn't in their motorcycle any more.

This is what the trace has to walk through: the whole family tree of LOT-VC-W29-03, straight from the vertex and edge tables, history and all. The red dashed links are the 8 packs the workshop took out, and the grey motorcycles are the 8 customers who would get a notice for nothing:

And this is what the four lines of openCypher make of it, as the app draws their answer: 27 units with their holders, 4 of them through the remanufactured packs, and not one of the 8 grey motorcycles:

How do I know the graph isn't just confidently wrong? Claude also wrote an oracle: a plain JavaScript walk over the same items and links, level by level, with no graph anywhere. For all 8 standard lots of week 29 the two agree exactly, unit by unit and holder by holder.

And speed? Doesn't matter at this size. In the spike the ABAP loop took 77 ms and the graph 67 ms. Now a warm trace answers in about 400 to 800 ms, through OData and all. Here is a screenshot from Postman:

 

The catch

There is one, and it's big if you live in ABAP Cloud.

  • The trace runs on A4H's own HANA, over a graph workspace that an AMDP method defines on two CDS view entities.
  • But openCypher won't go through an AMDP. ABAP's check rejects the SQL that HANA expands the query into: "The ABAP database schema ... cannot be specified explicitly". Uwe Fetzer ( @UweFetzer_se38 ) reported exactly this back in 2019, in his SAP Community question Opencypher in AMDP, and SAP called it a bug. I hit the same error on my release 816 system.
  • What does work is native SQL through ADBC (cl_sql_statement): SELECT ... FROM OPENCYPHER_TABLE( GRAPH WORKSPACE ... QUERY '...' ). ADBC is not released for ABAP Cloud, so this is classic ABAP only.
  • No query parameters either. The lot goes into the query text, so it's checked against a strict pattern first, and nothing but a lot number of the form LOT-VC-W29-03 gets through.
  • HANA 2.00.087 speaks a subset of openCypher: no named variable-length edge like [e*1..4], and one hop per pattern element. Hence the comma in the MATCH above.

The trace is a RAP custom entity, so to everyone else it's just another OData entity set.

 

Inside ZCL_RR_TRACE

The whole graph part lives in one class, ZCL_RR_TRACE. The graph itself is ten lines of it, an AMDP method that says which CDS view entity holds the vertices and which the edges:

METHOD graph BY DATABASE GRAPH WORKSPACE FOR HDB
  LANGUAGE SQL
  USING zi_rr_graphedge zi_rr_graphvertex.
  edge table zi_rr_graphedge
    source column sourceid
    target column targetid
    key    column edgeid
  vertex table zi_rr_graphvertex
    key    column vertexid
ENDMETHOD.

ZI_RR_GraphVertex reads the items, ZI_RR_GraphEdge the links. No copy of the data, no extra tables. Apart from that, the class does three jobs:

  1. It wakes the graph up. HANA creates an AMDP graph workspace only the first time an AMDP uses it, and our query comes in through ADBC. So before every query a tiny GraphScript procedure (HANA's own graph language) counts the vertices. The count goes nowhere - it's the wake-up call.
  2. It asks the question. Method UNITS checks the lot against the pattern, writes the four lines of openCypher into a string, wraps them in SELECT ... FROM OPENCYPHER_TABLE( GRAPH WORKSPACE "ZCL_RR_TRACE=>GRAPH" QUERY '...' ) and runs that through cl_sql_statement. The graph answers with units and holders only. Plain ABAP SQL then adds the model, the pack type, the delivery date, the current pack and the modules for the route text.
  3. It serves OData. The class implements IF_RAP_QUERY_PROVIDER, which makes it the query behind the custom entity ZI_RR_Trace. It takes exactly two filters, LotId eq and WithHistory eq, refuses any sorting, and does the paging itself.

 

The rest of the plumbing

Around the trace:

  • a RAP business object for the recall, in A4H: declare a lot defective, own the affected units (so two recalls never fight over one motorcycle), apply a remedy plan all or nothing,
  • in CAP, the plan and its rules: spare packs are scarce, so customers come first, and no motorcycle in stock gets a pack while a customer waits for one,
  • a Recall Agent who proposes a plan, explains it, and waits for an approver before anything reaches A4H,
  • a Recall section in the app, with the trace drawn as a graph and a button that opens the existing battery shortage scenario. One defect, two directions: back to who is affected, forward to what the shortage stops.

This is the trace of LOT-VC-W29-03 in the app, with the fleet customer CUS-FLEET-2 clicked: its routes light up in blue and everything else fades. 3 motorcycles, one of them through the remanufactured pack PCK-R0002, whose line stays orange. The modules are tucked into the lines from the lot to the packs:

In the first end-to-end run, the Recall Agent (Claude Sonnet 5) got LOT-VC-W29-03: 23 customer motorcycles, 3 in stock, 1 spare pack, 4 routes through remanufactured packs, and 16 free spare packs to go round. About 50 seconds later he was waiting for approval, with a plan:

  • 16 customers get a replacement pack now,
  • 7 get a notice and wait,
  • the 3 motorcycles in stock are blocked,
  • the affected spare pack is scrapped,
  • 10 packs need new supply from VoltCell, which in the Supply Chain Rescue world is blocked.

He also explained why one of the 6 fleet motorcycles, delivered two weeks after the other 5, doesn't jump the queue: "bumping it ahead of earlier-committed customers isn't justified by any stated operational need".

On the trace, a plan shows in colour: green gets a new pack now, purple waits for new supply, with the delivery date that decides who comes first. This is the bottom of the motorcycles column for that plan, the same as the rule plan. VIN-CARGO-31034, delivered on 6 August, waits in purple, while the other fleet motorcycles from 23 July get their packs:

Did the Agent do anything the rule plan didn't? Not this time: 0 units differ. After Approve, the plan was applied in A4H in 5.5 seconds.

Then Claude ran it again for the screenshots: same lot, same world, same Model. And this time that fleet motorcycle did jump the queue:

 

2 units differ from the rule plan: the fleet motorcycle VIN-CARGO-31034 got PCK-003635, the pack the rule plan gives to VIN-CITY-29118, and VIN-CITY-29118 waits instead. The Agent's reason: fleet vehicles "see higher daily mileage/usage and are safety-prioritized for scarce replacement packs ahead of equally-dated non-fleet customers".

Equally dated? VIN-CITY-29118 was delivered on 23 July, VIN-CARGO-31034 on 6 August. And Approve? Claude clicked it, taking the screenshots for me in the browser, without checking the dates either.

So which rule did the Agent break? None, strictly speaking. The delivery date is only the order the rule plan goes by. What the app enforces is that customers come before motorcycles in stock and that no spare pack sits idle while someone waits, and A4H checks the rest when the plan is applied. Fleet first is even allowed: the Agent's instructions say he may change which customers get the scarce packs, "for example fleet motorcycles in daily use first", as long as he explains every difference from the rule plan. He did explain it. The explanation was just wrong.

What could be changed after seeing this? For example: show the delivery dates of the units that differ on the card, have CAP check the dates the rationale claims, or leave the app as it is and make sure a person reads the units that differ.

 

So, was the graph useful?

Not because of speed. At this size it decides nothing, and a plain loop keeps up. On the query, the recall question is four lines of openCypher, and the difference between the right notices and 8 wrong ones on top is one condition in those four lines. The catch is the platform: classic ABAP only, through native SQL, until the AMDP bug is fixed.

And the Agent? He made a plan that passed every rule, in about 50 seconds, and in one of two runs explained it with dates that weren't true. The rules caught nothing because nothing was broken. The reason would still probably need a person who checks it against the data, thought.

 

P.S.: The setup was A4H, the 2025 Developer Trial (release 816 on HANA 2.00.087), in Docker on a VPS, reached through an SSH tunnel, and a Mac. Claude Code ran Opus 5.5 as the main Agent, with Haiku, Sonnet and Opus 5.5 sub-Agents, and talked to A4H through the vibing-steampunk MCP Server by Alice Vinogradova. Supply Chain Rescue runs CAP 10.1 on Node 24 and SAPUI5 1.136.8. The code: github.com/Kamilkov/supply-chain-rescue.

entry.title: CAP Agents that collaborates with humans - Announcing `cap-agents-sdm-backend` plugin
entry.content:
In my earlier articles, we explored how CAP agents can remember useful information across conversations and find relevant passages in documents using vector stores. But knowledge work often continues beyond finding an answer.

A project assistant or a manager may need to read last week's report, follow a reporting template, prepare this week's update, and save it where the team can review it. The result needs to become a document people can continue working with.

Enterprise Content Management has been a central piece in enterprises for document collaboration through role-based access control and audited work through versioning.

In this post, I'm introducing @mi8y/cap-agents-sdm-backend: an open-source add-on that lets CAP agents work on content and collaborate with humans via SAP Document Management or any compliant CMIS 1.1 repositories through an unified access layer.

SDM as a filesystem for knowledge work

With CAP v10 and the @cap-js/agents plugin, developers can build Calesi-pattern agents within CAP applications. CAP provides the application framework, while the underlying agent harness coordinates the model and its tools.

Tools such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex offer a useful illustration of this working style. An agent explores folders, reads instructions, finds relevant files, and saves its work. The filesystem gives it a practical way to organise and revisit content.

That pattern is useful for business content too. Imagine a workspace containing the following folder layout:

File content layout for agentic work

 The agent can read the instructions (AGENTS.md), discover how to prepare a report (via Agent Skills), inspect earlier work (previously created files), and write a new document. With this backend, the content lives in SAP Document Management rather than on the application's local disk, accessed as a virtual filesystem.

These file operations do not require a shell or a code-execution tool. Hence, this is a better and a more secured approach. The backend translates them into requests to the document repository via the CMIS 1.1 protocol.

A filesystem view for the agent, with content stored in SAP Document Management

@mi8y/cap-agents-sdm-backend implements the Deep Agents filesystem backend interface for SAP Document Management via CMIS Browser Binding. It is designed to be used with CAP Node.js 10 or later.

It gives the agent familiar operations to:

  • Browse folders and read files (ls command)
  • Create files, including missing parent folders below its configured workspace. (mkdir and >> operations)
  • Edit text within existing files (>> operation)
  • Find files by path patterns and search for literal text in their contents (grep command)

This is direct file access. This is in stark contrast to Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) through 'Semantic retrieval' using a vector store.

The CMIS Browser Binding approach also makes compatible CMIS repositories a possible backing store or virtual filesystem, subject to their supported capabilities and connection setup.

The source code is open-source and MIT licensed.

A shared workspace for people and agent collaboration

The most useful part is that the documents remain available with people too.

An agent can prepare a report, a team member (human) can review and revise it, and a later conversation can use the saved report as its starting point. The document becomes a shared work product that remains useful beyond the chat.

Content Management Interoperability Services v1.1 (CMIS) brings the content-management layer. Depending on the repository and configuration, this includes role-based access and document or folder permissions, version history, and the auditing capabilities. SAP's Document Management has in-built access controls and versioning for supported repositories.

Collaboration here means people and agents contributing to content in the same repository, through their respective interfaces i.e. UI for humans, while filesystem interface for agents.

People and agents collaborate together on documents

Example: Project Reporting Assistant

I added a basic reports assistant example in the repository demonstrating this pattern in a CAP application with an embedded SAPUI5 Document Management ReuseUI and an agent chat.

The workspace contains agent instructions, reporting skills, and templates. A user supplies a few updates:

Create this week's project status report for Northstar.

Integration testing is complete.
Environment access is still pending.
Carry forward the open actions from the previous report.

The agent reads the relevant instructions and template, consults the previous report, and saves a new text report in the repository. The user can then open the output report for review.

The example includes project status reports, incident reports, and executive briefings. For instance, an incident report can become the source for a later leadership briefing.

In the demo, instructions (AGENTS.md) and skills (Agent Skills) also live in SAP Document Management. Teams can update that content in the repository and start a new chat to load the revised instructions.

Team begins a conversation with an agent, and collaborates on the content

 Demo of Project Reporting Assistant

Getting started

Install the package in your CAP agent application:

npm install @mi8y/cap-agents-sdm-backend

The SdmBackend backend can automatically use the service-binding flow if having an SDM instance binding or can use a configured Cloud SDK destination. And the configured root folder lets the application expose a selected part of the repository as the agent's workspace.

There is no additional CDS persistence model or cds add step for document storage. The package README explains configuration, and the complete example shows the CAP integration and document UI.

Start with text-based content such as instructions, templates, and reports. Access to a file does not automatically provide native editing of Word documents, spreadsheets, or PDFs. Likewise, prompt instructions asking for confirmation or protecting templates need enforceable application controls when those are business requirements.

With this add-on, a CAP agent can leave behind more than a chat response: a report, a working draft, or an updated document that the team can pick up and continue.

Try the example, adapt the workspace to your use case, and share feedback or issues in the repository.
